response.answer: Yayoi Kusama, renowned for her iconic polka-dot art and immersive installations, passed away on August 27, 2026, at the age of 97. Her final decade was marked by a retreat from public life, yet her studio continued to produce her signature works. In the U.S., her art was on display at the Cincinnati Art Museum until October 18, 2026, featuring her "Infinity Mirror Room" and pumpkin paintings. Upcoming exhibitions include a major show at Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum starting September 11, 2026, and a retrospective in New York by David Zwirner in April showcasing her final decade's work.

results.title: The Mysterious and Lonely Final Decade of Yayoi Kusama’s Life
results.content:
In April, the gallerist David Zwirner will exhibit a selection of Kusama’s final works in New York.

“We’re so excited about the last decade,” the dealer said. “Arguably, this was the most extraordinary and successful decade of her career.”

It was also the most elusive, as the artist receded from view. [...] One of Kusama’s last public appearances was in 2017 at the opening of her museum in Tokyo. Longtime friends, curators and collectors said that she stopped receiving most guests in 2019 at the psychiatric hospital where she had lived for decades.

Yet her studio — a small group of assistants meant to carry out her artistic vision — was more prolific than ever, producing dozens of paintings and sculptures with her signature.

results.title: The Genius of Yayoi Kusama in Three Works
results.content:
In December 1963, Kusama showed her first known immersive installation, “Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show,” in a solo exhibition at Gertrude Stein Gallery, on Manhattan’s East 81st Street. [...] The mesmerizing art of Yayoi Kusama —who died in Tokyo on Aug. 14, at 97 — has in recent decades become ubiquitous, visible inblockbuster exhibitions and public spaces across the world,splashed across the facades of high-end luxury stores and snapped in thousands of selfies. But the characteristic motifs and themes — accumulation, infinity, love, life, death — of the artist born in 1929 in rural Japan, where creative expectations for women were nonexistent, have dominated her oeuvre since she [...] “I will keep painting until I die,” she told The Associated Press in 2012, and she did. Kusama also innovated across mediums including sculpture, installation, film, performance, fashion and literature. We look at three defining works in detail.

Photo of “Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show” installation in New York, featuring a rowboat ornamented with white soft-sculpture protrusions.

In them, a single element created a net-like pattern that seemed to continue beyond the frame. The reviews of the show, by the many of the most important critics of the time, were glowing. # Yayoi Kusama, Japan’s ‘queen of polka dots’, dies at 97

Kusama turned her hallucinations into work that ranged from dot-covered paintings and pumpkin sculptures to infinity mirror room installations.

Save

Share

FILE PHOTO: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama poses for a photograph inside her Infinity Mirrored Room installation titled [...] Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama in her Infinity Mirrored Room installation titled 'The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away' [File: Mike Segar/Reuters]



By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters

Published On 27 Aug 202627 Aug 2026

Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese artist known for her polka-dot paintings, pumpkin sculptures and immersive “Infinity Mirror Rooms”, has died at the age of 97. [...] As her fame grew, her international exhibitions attracted huge crowds and her works commanded lofty prices. One painting, Untitled (Nets) (1959), sold for $10.5m in 2022.

She received the Order of Culture, Japan’s highest honour for artists, in 2016.

David Zwirner, an art dealer who represented Kusama for 15 years, said she “was without a doubt the most famous living artist in the world” at the time of her passing.
